name: Bedrock Ocean Exploration
edge: Near-seafloor robots plus cloud survey infrastructure turn expensive ship campaigns into repeatable data.
summary: Autonomous underwater survey vehicles collect detailed seabed data, with cloud tools for mission coordination, processing, and customer delivery.
thesis: The interesting wedge is the complete survey operation: mobilization, reliable navigation, data quality, and usable deliverables. Bedrock couples its own underwater vehicles to survey software and trained regional operators. Multi-vehicle coverage could change the economics of repeatedly monitoring offshore energy assets, cables, and coastal infrastructure.
technology: Bedrock combines inertial navigation and Doppler velocity measurements with onboard data preprocessing and quality checks. Trident coordinates and monitors fleet missions; Mosaic processes, stores, and distributes geospatial survey data. Its published two-vehicle trial shows overlapping bathymetry and side-scan mosaics collected over adjacent survey sections. The scaling challenge includes launch and recovery, operator supervision, and cross-vehicle data consistency as much as robot autonomy.
problem: Detailed, repeatable seabed surveys require expensive vessel mobilization, specialist crews, reliable underwater positioning, and lengthy data processing. Offshore infrastructure needs current inspection-quality information rather than occasional coarse maps.

evidence.label: Technical field test
evidence.text: A company-published December 2023 two-AUV trial produced overlapping bathymetry and side-scan products; relative agreement in that test is not universal positioning accuracy.

evidence.label: Regional operations
evidence.text: August 6, 2026 announcement names First Marine Solutions as a multi-year partner, with an Aberdeen AUV hub and training for local survey operations.

Today’s IHO-quality positioning statement remains company-reported. Survey acceptance, vehicle recovery, weather, operator load, and mission economics need project-specific evidence; a public global ocean map is an ambition.

name: Rocsys
edge: Compliant connector handling automates the physical handoff between electric vehicles and charging systems.
summary: Vision-guided compliant robots plug electric port equipment and vehicle fleets into chargers, automating an infrastructure bottleneck.
thesis: A vehicle can drive itself and still need someone to connect its charging cable. Rocsys attacks this narrow but consequential physical interface. Heavy-duty terminal deployments create a practical entry point; its shared overhead robot for multiple robotaxi bays tests whether infrastructure automation can scale without one expensive arm per parking space.
technology: The S2 design combines a seven-axis motion architecture, camera-based six-degree-of-freedom inlet localization, compliance for vehicle movement, and electromagnetic connector locking. Industrial controls, APIs, and charging-service monitoring integrate the robot with fleet operations. The M1 uses an overhead rail and long-reach arm to serve multiple bays. This is precision connector manipulation under weather, alignment variation, and repeated high-duty-cycle operation.
problem: Manual cable connection interrupts electrified fleet operations and prevents unattended depot workflows. Port equipment and robotaxis need reliable charging without repeated labor, connector damage, or excessive idle time.

evidence.label: Named operational site
evidence.text: April 2026 company case names International Transportation Service at the Port of Long Beach, charging a human-operated electric Taylor container handler.

evidence.label: Pilot versus deployment
evidence.text: M1 was announced April 29, 2026 for up to ten bays; the announcement describes pilots and targets large-scale deployment in 2027.

Charging automation does not drive the vehicle or remove depot cleaning, inspection, and maintenance work. Published savings require utilization and labor assumptions; mixed connectors, reach limits, uptime, and exception handling must be validated at each site.

name: Kodama Systems
edge: Retrofit skidders combine satellite teleoperation and local perception to move skilled operators offsite.
summary: Retrofit controls let skilled operators run forestry skidders remotely, with edge perception and assisted autonomy for difficult logging sites.
thesis: Kodama targets the operational bottleneck around a specific forestry machine rather than trying to automate an entire forest immediately. Retrofitting established skidders preserves contractors’ equipment investments, while remote operation reduces commuting and cab exposure. Supervised autonomy could eventually let scarce skilled operators manage more equipment, but that economic step needs separate proof.
technology: RS1 adds satellite video and telemetry links, HDR cameras, LiDAR, rugged onboard computing, localization, and machine-state monitoring to existing equipment. A separate emergency-stop and hold-to-run circuit sits outside application software. Remote operators retain the machine’s core controls and local crews handle servicing. Published field accounts cover remote skidding; current product material and Weyerhaeuser reporting describe AI-assisted navigation and terrain mapping toward supervised autonomy.
problem: Logging contractors face scarce equipment operators, remote job sites, strenuous cab work, and dangerous terrain. Forest restoration and timber extraction need more productive machine hours without worsening operator exposure or fatigue.

evidence.label: Field-tested retrofit
evidence.text: Company accounts describe two seasons on a CAT 525C in the Stanislaus National Forest and subsequent Weiler S340 operations; these are vendor-reported field deployments.

evidence.label: Named industrial pilot
evidence.text: April 23, 2026 WSJ reporting describes a Weyerhaeuser pilot using remote operation with AI-assisted navigation; full autonomy remains a goal.

Operators and local crews still matter; radio/satellite reliability, terrain feedback, recovery, and machine servicing affect economics. Company demonstration throughput is not a universal benchmark, and forest carbon-storage ambitions are separate from verified logging productivity.

name: Verity
edge: Small indoor drone fleets reconcile the warehouse’s physical stock with its digital system of record.
summary: GPS-free indoor drones scan warehouse inventory and reconcile physical stock with warehouse systems, exposing misplaced pallets and record errors.
thesis: Verity’s valuable output is inventory certainty, not drone flight. Lightweight robots reach high storage locations and continuously collect observations that reconcile with warehouse records. Its live-events robotics lineage has translated into customer-confirmed logistics deployments, making it an unusually concrete example of embodied sensing becoming an operational data product.
technology: Onboard perception, motion planning, obstacle avoidance, cameras, and lighting support autonomous indoor flights without GPS. Drones scan barcodes and return to charging stations while a cloud platform coordinates fleet operations and integrates observations into warehouse management systems. Physical-to-digital reconciliation identifies missing or misplaced goods. IKEA describes scheduled missions and newer flights alongside workers; the commercial navigation and fleet stack remain proprietary.
problem: Warehouse databases drift from physical reality as pallets move, barcodes are missed, and items are misplaced. Manual high-rack checks consume labor, create ergonomic strain, and discover errors too late for fulfillment.

evidence.label: Customer-verified scale
evidence.text: IKEA’s August 2024 account reported 250+ drones at 73 locations in nine countries and tested operation alongside workers. These counts describe that dated snapshot.

evidence.label: Current industry recognition
evidence.text: June 2026 IFR/IEEE IERA award material describes about 200 warehouse deployments, onboard autonomy, barcode integration, and fleet learning.

sources.note: Primary customer source describes scale, missions, obstacle rerouting, and a one-year Belgian test. The planned US rollout is distinct from achieved deployment.

sources.title: IFR — 2026 IERA robotics award
sources.note: Industry award body describes current system and about 200 warehouses. Operational numbers are reported award evidence, not a disclosed independent audit.

sources.note: Primary customer documents a launch, WMS/API integration, and initial estimates. Potential savings are not universal ROI; one section requires an account.

sources.note: Research institution describes technical lineage, barcode capture, charging, and commercialization; historical 2021 context.

sources.note: December 2024 first-person founder essay names Markus Hehn and Markus Waibel, and explains autonomy, reliability, data economics, and cloud architecture. Self-reported performance remains attributed.

sources.note: A self-identified former shipping/receiving worker describes inventory-counting pain; other comments raise noise and job concerns. Identity and claims are not independently verified.

caveat: Inventory sensing does not pick products or repair an inaccurate workflow automatically. Barcode visibility, occlusions, configuration, integration, and battery replacement still matter. Dated IKEA fleet counts differ from company-wide warehouse counts. Vendor ROI and reliability claims need customer-specific baselines; the commercial stack is not open source.

name: Fulfil Solutions
edge: Engineered trays and fixed dispensers simplify variable grocery handling before mobile robots collect bags.
summary: Purpose-built trays, dispensers, and mobile ShopBots assemble grocery orders across ambient, refrigerated, and frozen storage zones.
thesis: The differentiated bet is to redesign storage and handling together rather than make a general robot pick arbitrary shelves. Item-level tracking and controlled dispensing can make delicate produce, expiry management, and mixed-temperature grocery orders tractable. A customer-confirmed Whole Foods installation makes the systems architecture more interesting than an isolated picking demo.
technology: Dense item-level trays stack in vertical storage towers. Fixed dispense stations retrieve trays and use custom actuators, vision, and sensor fusion to place items into bags carried by mobile ShopBots. Routing and packing order reduce damage while station inventory redistribution balances load. Refrigerated enclosures handle fresh and frozen goods. Published patents explain tray, carousel, inspection, and dispensing embodiments; those embodiments are not proof of every deployed mechanism.
problem: Online grocery fulfillment combines thin margins with fragile, variable-shaped goods, expiry constraints, and multiple temperature zones. Manual picking and unsuitable general warehouse automation make reliable, affordable order assembly difficult.

evidence.label: Customer-confirmed installation
evidence.text: Amazon’s May 12, 2026 update describes Fulfil ShopBots in a 10,000-square-foot Plymouth Meeting Whole Foods facility supporting approximately 12,000 items.

evidence.label: Human workflow boundary
evidence.text: The same customer account says employees finalize orders at handoff. Automated picking and packing do not establish an entirely labor-free store or delivery operation.

caveat: A named grocery deployment does not prove profitable economics across store formats. Restocking, exceptions, cleaning, maintenance, handoff, and delivery still require consideration. Investor accuracy figures lack public test denominators. Patent embodiments exceed demonstrated functionality, and Fulfil Solutions should not be confused with the unrelated fulfil.io ERP company.
